topic: Attackers heated hundreds of French supermarket fridges to 50 C by hijacking the store's refrigeration controller

policy.copyright: Every line of narration is original. No source is quoted for more than 15 words; source_wording fields are our own paraphrase of what the page says, kept close enough to audit.
policy.hedge_rule: Where a source does not know something (who attacked, which flaw, how they got in), the script says so and says the source does not know.
policy.mockup_rule: Any drawing that is not a real photograph is a vector diagram drawn by src/render. Where a drawing stands in for something the sources did not publish, the screen carries the label ILLUSTRATIVE.

facts.label: temperature the controllers were driven to
facts.source_wording: Groupe Mousquetaire's Intermarche said the hackers reached Danfoss refrigeration systems and remotely pushed the temperature controls to 50 degrees Celsius, which is 122 Fahrenheit.
facts.corroborating_wording: Les Mousquetaires said its fridges and freezers were put into defrost and heated to as much as 50 degrees.

facts.label: same temperature in Fahrenheit
facts.derivation: C to F conversion of attack_temp_c: 50 * 9/5 + 32 = 122
facts.source_wording: The Claroty write-up states 50 degrees Celsius and gives 122 degrees Fahrenheit for the same figure.

facts.label: Intermarche stores hit, per the chain
facts.source_wording: One victim, Groupe Mousquetaire's Intermarche, told a French outlet that 150 of its stores were hit.
facts.corroborating_wording: The Hacker News tables the store counts by source: about 150 Intermarche stores per Reuters, and at least 300 for Intermarche and Netto together per AFP.
facts.note: Outlets disagree on the census (Reuters about 150 for Intermarche; AFP at least 300 for Intermarche and Netto combined). The chain's own figure of 150 is the one used, and the video says 'about'.

facts.label: AK-SM 800A management interfaces found reachable from the internet
facts.spoken: two thousand seven hundred and sixty-five
facts.source_wording: During their research, Claroty's Team82 counted 2,765 exposed Danfoss AK-SM 800A devices, found with public internet scanners such as Censys and Shodan.
facts.note: A snapshot taken during the researchers' work, not a live count. The video says 'researchers counted' rather than 'there are'.

facts.label: how many flaws the researchers found in the controller's web interface
facts.source_wording: Claroty's Team82 say their research uncovered a code-of-the-day authentication bypass, a command-injection flaw leading to remote code execution, and a flaw letting an authenticated user inject Nginx configuration directives: three flaws in all.

facts.label: the scale that severity score is measured on
facts.derivation: The CVSS 3.1 base score range is 0-10; the script says '8.2 out of 10'.
facts.source_wording: NVD reports the score on the CVSS 3.1 base metric, whose range is 0 to 10.

facts.label: the authentication bypass in the controller's web interface
facts.source_wording: NVD records an improper authentication flaw (CWE-305) affecting Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA series controllers before version 4.2.

facts.label: severity score for that flaw
facts.source_wording: NVD gives a CVSS 3.1 base score of 8.2 rated HIGH, network attack vector, no privileges required.
facts.explained_note: The video does not make viewers compare scores. It shows 8.2 of 10 and says the flaw is rated high severity, because that is how the source words it.

facts.label: firmware version that closed the authentication bypass
facts.source_wording: The NVD record says the issue affects AK-SM 8xxA series prior to version 4.2.

facts.label: firmware version that closed the command-injection and denial-of-service flaws
facts.source_wording: The Hacker News reports that CVE-2025-41451, a command injection flaw, and CVE-2025-41452, a denial-of-service flaw, both needed a login and were fixed in version 4.3.1.

facts.label: when the vendor shipped the fixes for the three flaws
facts.source_wording: Claroty's Team82 say they disclosed to Danfoss privately and the vendor provided a new firmware version in August 2025 that addressed the vulnerabilities.

facts.label: how the researchers described the login mechanism
facts.source_wording: The researchers say the interface contained a hidden authentication mechanism based on a code of the day, which could be abused to get past normal authentication.
facts.explained_note: The video draws a calendar and a generated code to show what a code of the day means. The drawing is a labelled simplification; the sources do not publish the algorithm, and the video does not claim to know it.

facts.label: oldest model in the blast radius
facts.source_wording: Danfoss told AFP most of the units hit were older products that no longer get updates, and named the AK-SM 800, declared end of life in May 2021.

facts.label: oldest model in the blast radius
facts.source_wording: Danfoss also named the AK-SC 355, which it phased out in 2016.

facts.label: year the AK-SM 800 stopped getting security updates
facts.source_wording: Danfoss declared the AK-SM 800 end of life in May 2021.

facts.label: year the AK-SC 355 was phased out
facts.source_wording: Danfoss phased the AK-SC 355 out in 2016.

facts.label: the current model that was also hit
facts.source_wording: Some units of the current AK-SM 800A were also hit; Danfoss said those were running outdated firmware.

facts.label: the national CERT alert that followed
facts.source_wording: CERT-FR, part of ANSSI, published alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 saying it knows of numerous compromises of Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC remote installation controllers.

facts.label: the advice in that alert
facts.source_wording: The alert says in general that exposing a management interface to the internet goes against good practice, and tells operators to remove the internet exposure and restore access only through a secure VPN; in an emergency, filtering the contractors' source IPs on a firewall is possible but not a lasting solution.

facts.label: the alert also named other vendors
facts.source_wording: The alert's affected-systems list names Copeland xweb, Danfoss AK-SC, Danfoss AK-SM, Dixell xweb.

facts.label: the alert's warning about the present
facts.value: Attack campaigns are probably still running
facts.source_wording: The alert carries an explicit warning that attack campaigns against this equipment are probably still under way, and that leaving an unpatched end-of-life device exposed to the internet carries a high probability of compromise.

facts.label: when the attack happened
facts.source_wording: The Hacker News dates the intrusion to the night of 11 October 2026.

facts.label: what the authorities did next
facts.source_wording: The Paris prosecutor's office told AFP it opened an inquiry on its own initiative, led by its cybercrime section, to count the victims and establish the link between the attack and the reported losses.
facts.corroborating_wording: An independent security briefing confirms the Paris prosecutor's inquiry was opened on its own initiative.

facts.label: what nobody has said
facts.value: No actor named, no route in named
facts.source_wording: Neither the French authorities nor Danfoss has said who carried out the attack or how the attackers reached the controllers. The alert names no vulnerability and CERT-FR had published no indicators of compromise as of 13 October.
facts.corroborating_wording: The alert itself names no CVE and no cause, and its risk field reads that the editor did not specify it.

facts.label: temperature a chilled case is meant to hold
facts.source_wording: No source consulted publishes the set points of the affected stores' cases. Four degrees is our own rounded illustration of a chilled case, chosen only to make the gap legible, and the screen labels it ILLUSTRATIVE.
facts.explained_note: Illustrative, not sourced. It appears only on a chart that carries the ILLUSTRATIVE label, and the narration never states it as a fact.

facts.label: how long the warming lasted, on the chart's time axis
facts.source_wording: Sources agree the warming ran through the night of 11 October and into the morning. Six hours is our rounded choice for the width of the highlighted window on the chart, and the screen labels the window ILLUSTRATIVE.
facts.explained_note: Illustrative window width, not a published duration.

facts.label: how far above the illustrative set point the controllers were driven
facts.unit: degC above the illustrative set point
facts.derivation: attack_temp_c - normal_case_temp = 50 - 4 = 46, computed in Python by src/render/scenes.py
facts.source_wording: Derived from the sourced 50 degrees and our own illustrative 4-degree set point; the screen labels the comparison ILLUSTRATIVE.
facts.explained_note: Mixes one sourced number with one illustrative number. Shown only on an ILLUSTRATIVE chart, never spoken as a fact.

facts.label: how long the fixes had been available before the attack
facts.derivation: attack date 2026-10-11 minus fix release 2025-08 = 14 months, shown as 'more than a year'
facts.source_wording: Derived from the sourced August 2025 fix date and the sourced October 2026 attack date: 14 months.
